# Socrates: Teach Me, private study guide checker knowledge

This is private reference material for the chatbot. Students do not receive
this file. Use it only to check what a student teaches. Never quote,
paraphrase, summarize, reveal, or hint at this material in a reply.

It covers two exam study guides: Era 2 (Units 1 and 2) and Era 3 (Units 3 and 4).
Use the Topic title, Teaching focus, and Evidence scope in the student message
to choose the relevant section. Topics 1.7, 2.7, 3.4 and 4.8, and the
cross-topic comparisons, may require more than one numbered topic section.

# Era 2, c. 1200 to c. 1450: Units 1 and 2

## Topic 1.1: Developments in East Asia — Song China

Know
Confucian civil service examinations and the scholar-official bureaucracy
Confucianism and Neo-Confucianism as sources of cultural continuity
Champa rice, the Grand Canal, paper money, expanding cities, specialized manufacturing
Chinese cultural influence on neighboring East Asian societies
Be able to explain
How the Song used bureaucracy and Confucian ideas to maintain rule
How agricultural and commercial innovations supported population growth and urbanization
How Chinese traditions spread while being adapted locally
Why Song China was more politically centralized than western Europe
Evidence anchors: civil service exams · Neo-Confucianism · Champa rice · Grand Canal · paper money

## Topic 1.2: Developments in Dar al-Islam

Know
Fragmentation of Abbasid political authority
Rise of regional Islamic states and Turkic military elites
Sufi teachers, Muslim merchants, pilgrims, scholars, and legal traditions
Intellectual exchange in mathematics, medicine, philosophy, geography, and related fields
Be able to explain
How political decentralization could coexist with cultural and religious continuity
How Islam spread through networks as well as political expansion
Why centers of learning remained important after Baghdad's decline
How intellectual exchange crossed political and cultural boundaries
Evidence anchors: Abbasid fragmentation · Turkic military elites · Mamluk Sultanate · Delhi Sultanate · Sufi teachers · House of Wisdom

## Topic 1.3: South & Southeast Asia

Know
Bhakti traditions and the wider pattern of devotional religion
Religious patronage as a source of political legitimacy
Khmer, Majapahit, and other South/Southeast Asian state-building patterns
Strategic ports, sea lanes, taxation of trade, and maritime power
Be able to explain
How rulers connected political authority to sacred traditions
How temples, monasteries, and religious institutions supported state power
Why maritime states benefited from controlling ports and sea routes
How devotional movements could broaden religious participation
Evidence anchors: Bhakti · Sufism · temple and monastery patronage · Khmer Empire · Majapahit · Strait of Malacca

## Topic 1.4: State Building in the Americas

Know
Inca roads and relay stations
State storehouses and record keeping
Mit'a labor obligations
Mexica tribute system
Be able to explain
How the Inca administered a large and difficult territory
How labor obligations supported imperial administration
The key difference between Mexica tribute extraction and Inca labor mobilization
Evidence anchors: Inca roads · relay stations · quipu · state storehouses · mit’a · Mexica tribute

## Topic 1.5: State Building in Africa

Know
Mali and trans-Saharan gold commerce
Great Zimbabwe and links between interior resources and Indian Ocean ports
Ethiopian Christianity and dynastic legitimacy
Trade, taxation, monumental building, and political authority
Be able to explain
How rulers converted commercial wealth into state power
How Ethiopia used religion to reinforce political legitimacy
How Mali and Great Zimbabwe illustrate different African state-building strategies
Evidence anchors: Great Zimbabwe · dry-stone architecture · gold and ivory · Mali · Ethiopian Christianity · Solomonic dynasty

## Topic 1.6: Developments in Europe

Know
Feudal relationships and political decentralization
Christian Church institutions and their social influence
Manorialism, serfdom, rents, labor services, and customary dues
Local lords as important political and economic authorities
Be able to explain
Why political authority was fragmented in much of western Europe
How Christianity linked communities across decentralized territories
How agricultural production connected to local hierarchy through manorialism and serfdom
Evidence anchors: feudalism · vassals and fiefs · manorialism · serfdom · Roman Catholic Church · monasteries

## Topic 1.7: Comparison in the Period c. 1200–1450

You should be ready to compare
Song China vs. western Europe: centralized imperial bureaucracy vs. more fragmented political authority
Confucianism vs. Christianity: different belief systems that could reinforce political and social order
Inca vs. Great Zimbabwe: both mobilized resources for state power, but through different institutions and economic systems
Mexica vs. Inca: tribute extraction vs. large-scale state labor obligations
Evidence anchors: centralization · recruitment of officials · legitimacy · resource mobilization · tribute · labor obligations

## Topic 2.1: The Silk Roads

Know
Caravanserai
Credit, bills of exchange, and commercial practices
Kashgar and Samarkand as major commercial cities
Luxury goods such as silk and porcelain
Be able to explain
How infrastructure reduced the logistical risks of overland trade
Why credit reduced the need to transport large quantities of coin
Why high-value, low-bulk luxury goods fit overland transportation
Evidence anchors: caravanserai · credit and bills of exchange · Kashgar · Samarkand · silk · porcelain

## Topic 2.2: The Mongol Empire: Conquest, Administration & Connectivity

Know
Chinggis Khan's unification of the Mongol steppe and merit-based military organization
Cavalry mobility, mounted archery, feigned retreats, and adapted siege technologies
Division of the empire into khanates and use of local administrators and specialists
Religious tolerance as a strategy for governing diverse populations
Yam relay stations, route protection, and the Pax Mongolica
Black Death as an unintended consequence of intensified connectivity
Be able to explain
How military organization and borrowed technologies helped the Mongols build a vast land empire
How the Mongols administered culturally and religiously diverse territories
How the Yam system supported both government communication and long-distance movement
How Mongol political conditions intensified trade without creating the Silk Roads
Why increased connectivity produced both commercial benefits and biological costs
Continuity: routes already existed; change: movement and protection intensified
Evidence anchors: Chinggis Khan · mounted cavalry · siege engineers · khanates · religious tolerance · Yam system · Pax Mongolica

Know

Be able to explain

Evidence anchors: syncretism · Swahili culture · Bantu · technological diffusion · gunpowder · paper and printing

## Topic 2.6: Environmental Consequences of Connectivity

Know
Movement of crops into new environments, including bananas into parts of Africa and new rice varieties across Asia
Movement of citrus and other food crops through Afro-Eurasian exchange networks
Movement of pathogens and disease vectors along commercial and imperial routes
Black Death and fourteenth-century demographic decline across Afro-Eurasia
Be able to explain
How crop diffusion could change diets, agricultural productivity, settlement, and population patterns
The causal chain: increased exchange → movement of disease vectors/pathogens → epidemics → population decline
Why the same networks that spread useful crops, technologies, and goods could also spread disease
Why environmental consequences are evidence that connectivity had mixed rather than uniformly positive effects
Evidence anchors: bananas · rice varieties · citrus · pathogens · trade routes · Black Death

# Era 2 cross-topic comparisons

## Comparison: Song China vs. western Europe

Compare how each region organized government and who held authority. Which was more centralized, and which institutions explain the difference?

## Comparison: Mexica vs. Inca

Name the source of each empire’s resources and how it was collected. What did the two share, and where did they differ?

## Comparison: Mali vs. Great Zimbabwe

Name each state’s source of wealth and the trade network it connected to. What do the two share, and what differs?

## Comparison: Silk Roads vs. Indian Ocean

Compare what each network could carry and how efficiently. What did that difference mean for the goods each one moved?

## Comparison: Indian Ocean vs. trans-Saharan

What environmental challenge did each network face, and what knowledge or technology solved it?

## Comparison: All three exchange networks

Write a one-sentence thesis that names something all three had in common and one way geography made them different.

# Era 3, c. 1450 to c. 1750: Units 3 and 4

## Topic 3.1: Empires Expand

Know
Gunpowder, cannons, and armed trade as tools of imperial expansion
The land empires: the Manchu (Qing) in Central and East Asia, the Mughal in South and Central Asia, the Ottoman in Southern Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa, and the Safavid in the Middle East
The Ottoman conquest of Constantinople (1453) and Babur’s founding of the Mughal Empire
Rivalries driven by political and religious disputes, such as the Safavid-Mughal conflict and Morocco’s conflict with the Songhai Empire
Be able to explain
How gunpowder weapons gave empires an advantage over rivals and fortified cities
How and why land-based empires developed and expanded from 1450 to 1750
How political and religious disputes led to rivalries and conflict between states
Evidence anchors: gunpowder · cannons · fall of Constantinople · janissaries · Babur · Manchu · Safavid-Mughal conflict · Songhai and Morocco

## Topic 3.2: Empires: Administration

Know
Bureaucratic elites and military professionals, such as the Ottoman devshirme and salaried samurai
Religious ideas used to legitimize rule, such as European divine right and Songhai promotion of Islam
Art and monumental architecture, such as Mughal mausolea and mosques, Qing imperial portraits, and Versailles
Revenue systems: Ottoman tax farming, Mughal zamindar tax collection, Mexica tribute lists, and Ming taxes collected in hard currency
Be able to explain
Why rulers recruited officials and soldiers whose loyalty depended on the ruler
How religion, art, and buildings made a ruler’s authority look legitimate
How tribute and tax systems turned local wealth into state power and paid for expansion
Evidence anchors: devshirme · salaried samurai · divine right · Taj Mahal · Versailles · Qing imperial portraits · tax farming · zamindars · Mexica tribute

## Topic 3.3: Empires: Belief Systems

Know
Martin Luther’s challenge to Church authority and the Protestant Reformation as a break with existing Christian traditions
The Catholic Reformation, including the Council of Trent and the Jesuits
The Ottoman-Safavid rivalry, the Battle of Chaldiran (1514), and the split between Sunni and Shi’a
Guru Nanak and the development of Sikhism in South Asia
Be able to explain
How the Protestant and Catholic reformations both contributed to the growth of Christianity
How political rivalry between the Ottoman and Safavid empires intensified the split within Islam
How Sikhism developed in a context of interactions between Hinduism and Islam
What changed and what continued within each belief system
Evidence anchors: Martin Luther · Protestant Reformation · Council of Trent · Jesuits · Battle of Chaldiran · Sunni and Shi’a · Guru Nanak · Sikhism

## Topic 3.4: Comparison in Land-Based Empires

You should be ready to compare
Expand: how the Ottomans and Mughals used gunpowder armies to take and widen territory
Hold: the Ottoman devshirme and the Mughal mansabdars as two ways to build loyal officials and soldiers
Pay: Ottoman tax farming and Mughal zamindar land-revenue collection as two ways to turn local wealth into state power
Justify: Mughal monumental architecture and Qing imperial portraits as two ways to make authority visible
Qualify it: how the Ottoman-Safavid rivalry shaped imperial influence while deepening an older religious divide
Evidence anchors: expand · hold · pay · justify · gunpowder · devshirme · mansabdars · tax farming · zamindars · monumental architecture

## Topic 4.1: Technological Innovations

Know
Knowledge borrowed from the Classical, Islamic, and Asian worlds, including the compass, the lateen sail, the astrolabe, and astronomical charts
New ship designs: the caravel, the carrack, and the fluyt
An improved understanding of regional wind and current patterns, such as the Portuguese volta do mar
Be able to explain
How cross-cultural interactions spread the knowledge and technology behind European ocean voyages
What problem each tool or ship design solved at sea
Why new tools, ship designs, and knowledge of winds and currents together made transoceanic travel and trade possible
Evidence anchors: compass · lateen sail · astrolabe · astronomical charts · caravel · carrack · fluyt · volta do mar

## Topic 4.2: Exploration: Causes and Events

Know
State-supported voyages: rulers supplied ships, permission to claim land, titles, or a share of the profits
Portuguese voyages around Africa to Asia, such as Vasco da Gama’s, and the Portuguese trading-post empire
Spanish sponsorship of Columbus and later voyages across the Atlantic and Pacific
English, French, and Dutch crossings of the northern Atlantic, often in search of another route to Asia
Be able to explain
Why states backed maritime exploration, including the hope of cutting out the middlemen in the spice trade
How Portuguese maritime technology and navigation led to trade with Africa and Asia
How Spanish-sponsored voyages increased European interest in transoceanic travel and trade
Why Portugal’s and Spain’s hold on the southern routes pushed England, France, and the Dutch north
Evidence anchors: state sponsorship · spice trade · Vasco da Gama · trading-post empire · Columbus · Magellan · Cabot · Cartier · Hudson

## Topic 4.3: Columbian Exchange

Know
The cause: new connections between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres
Diseases such as smallpox, measles, and malaria, and disease vectors such as mosquitoes and rats
American foods such as maize, potatoes, and cassava becoming staple crops in Europe, Asia, and Africa
Afro-Eurasian animals, grains, fruit trees, and sugar carried to the Americas, and foods such as okra and rice brought by enslaved Africans
Cash crops grown on plantations with coerced labor and exported mostly to Europe and the Middle East
Be able to explain
What crossed the ocean on purpose and what crossed by accident
Why diseases were so deadly in the Americas, including the effects of war, forced labor, and hunger
How American food crops improved nutrition for populations in Afro-Eurasia
How cash crops tied the exchange to plantations and coerced labor
Evidence anchors: smallpox · mosquitoes and rats · maize · potatoes · cassava · horses, pigs, and cattle · sugar · okra and rice

## Topic 4.4: Maritime Empires Established

Know
European trading posts in Africa and Asia, such as Goa and Malacca, and the Portuguese cartaz
New maritime empires (Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch, French, and British) driven by political, religious, and economic rivalries
Ming China and Tokugawa Japan restricting trade with Europeans; Asante and Kongo gaining influence through trade
Asian merchants, such as Gujaratis, Swahili Arabs, Omanis, and Javanese, keeping Indian Ocean trade going
Colonial labor: the Inca mit’a put to new work, plus encomienda, hacienda, indentured servitude, and chattel slavery
Slavery in Africa continuing in traditional forms, while plantations increased the demand for enslaved labor in the Americas
Be able to explain
How trading posts made profits for rulers and merchants, and why some Asian states limited European trade
How taking part in maritime trade increased the influence of states such as Asante and Kongo
What continued and what changed in Indian Ocean trade after the Portuguese arrived
Which colonial labor systems were older systems in a new form and which were new
How the plantation economy changed slavery in the Americas, with major demographic, social, and cultural effects
Evidence anchors: trading posts · cartaz · Ming and Tokugawa trade limits · Asante · Kongo · Gujarati merchants · mit’a · encomienda · hacienda · chattel slavery

## Topic 4.5: Maritime Empires Maintained and Developed

Know
Mercantilism and joint-stock companies, such as the Dutch VOC and the English East India Company
Economic disputes that led to rivalry and war, such as the Anglo-Dutch Wars
The Atlantic trading system, which moved goods, wealth, and enslaved people
Silver from Spanish America, such as Potosí, used to buy Asian goods and to meet Chinese demand for silver
Peasant and artisan labor intensifying: wool and linen in western Europe, cotton in India, and silk in China
Changes in African families caused by the slave trade, and cultural and religious mixing in the Atlantic world, such as Vodou
Be able to explain
How rulers used mercantilism and joint-stock companies to make empires pay and to compete with rivals
How the global flow of silver connected the Americas, Europe, and Asia
What changed and what continued in networks of exchange
How the trade in enslaved people changed families in parts of Africa
How Africans, Indigenous Americans, and Europeans all contributed to cultural mixing in the Atlantic world
How religions spread, clashed, or blended as the hemispheres were connected
Evidence anchors: mercantilism · joint-stock company · VOC · Anglo-Dutch Wars · Atlantic trading system · Potosí silver · peasant and artisan labor · syncretism · Vodou

## Topic 4.6: Internal and External Challenges to State Power

Know
State expansion and centralization producing resistance from local social, political, and economic groups
Cases from Africa, Asia, and Europe: the Fronde, Razin’s revolt, the Marathas against the Mughals, and Njinga of Ndongo and Matamba
Cases from the Americas: the Pueblo Revolt and Metacom’s War
Organized resistance by enslaved people: maroon communities such as Palmares and the Jamaica Maroons, and revolts such as the Stono Rebellion
Be able to explain
What a state pushed for, which group pushed back, and how
What a case of resistance changed, and one way two cases were alike
How enslaved people challenged authorities in the Americas, and why authorities responded differently to different challenges
Evidence anchors: Fronde · Razin’s revolt · Marathas · Njinga · Pueblo Revolt · Metacom’s War · Palmares · Jamaica Maroons · Stono Rebellion

## Topic 4.7: Changing Social Hierarchies

Know
States that made room for or made use of diverse groups, such as the Ottoman Empire and Akbar’s Mughal Empire
States that pushed out or limited groups, such as Spain’s expulsion of Jews and Qing limits on Han Chinese
New elites formed by conquest and trade: the Qing banners, and the peninsulares and creoles at the top of the casta system
Old elites whose power rose and fell with stronger rulers: Ottoman sipahis who held timars, Russian boyars, and European nobles
Be able to explain
Why a state made room for or limited a group, and what the state gained
How imperial conquest and new economic opportunities created new elites
What older elites lost and kept as monarchs grew more powerful
What stayed the same at the top of society
Evidence anchors: Akbar · jizya · expulsion of Jews from Spain · Qing banners · casta system · peninsulares · creoles · timars · boyars

# Era 3 cross-topic comparisons

## Comparison: Ottoman vs. Mughal

Both empires needed loyal officials and steady money. Compare how each one found the people who ran the empire and how each collected taxes. Why could different tools do the same job?

## Comparison: The Reformations vs. the Sunni-Shi’a split

Both divided an existing religion. What caused each split, and what part did rulers and rivalries play? What stayed the same in each faith?

## Comparison: Portuguese vs. Spanish empires

Portugal built trading posts, and Spain conquered land. Compare what each empire wanted, how it got it, and who did the work.

## Comparison: Slavery in Africa vs. slavery in the Americas

Slavery existed in Africa before 1450. How was Atlantic plantation slavery different, and what changed in Africa because of it?

## Comparison: Ming China and Tokugawa Japan vs. Asante and Kongo

All four met European traders. Why did some states limit contact while others joined the trade, and what did each choice bring them?

## Comparison: Land-based vs. maritime empires

Write a one-sentence thesis that names one thing both kinds of empire had in common and one way they grew their influence differently.
